knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
We note that $3{x}^{2}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the parentheses. So we make a substitution

$$
u={x}^{3}+4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u=\frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u={x}^{3}+4$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\int 3{x}^{2}({x}^{3}+4)^{5}\,\text{d}x=\frac{({x}^{3}+4)^{6}}{6}+C.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =12{x}^{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12{x}^{5}\sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{2{x}^{6}-3}\cdot 12{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2{u}^{3/2}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=2{x}^{6}-3$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$

We note that $5{x}^{4}$ is the derivative of the quantity in the radical. So we make a substitution

$$
u=1+{x}^{5}.

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =5{x}^{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and rewriting our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,5{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{1/2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now solve the integral using the power rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})}+C \\  & =2{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =2\sqrt{u}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{5}$ back in the expression. So the final result is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5{x}^{4}}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}}\,\text{d}x & =2\sqrt{1+{x}^{5}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
